Learning Objectives
Describe the epidemiology, anatomy, and biomechanics of the anterior cruciate ligament.
Identify key features of the evaluation of the anterior cruciate ligament, including physical
examination and imaging study findings.
List indications for surgical management of anterior cruciate ligament injuries and techniques
for reconstruction.
Review potential complications, rehabilitation, and outcomes associated with anterior cruciate
ligament injury.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview

The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is most commonly injured during sports-related activity;
however, some ACL injuries result from high-energy trauma or activities of daily living.
Approximately 70% of patients hear or feel a pop at the time of injury.1

Overview
Almost all patients notice swelling of the knee within 6 to 12 hours postinjury. ACL
injuries may be classified as occurring from a noncontact or contact mechanism of
injury. Noncontact injuries usually occur during cutting or pivoting. ACL injuries are
commonly sustained during soccer, football, basketball, and gymnastics. They also more
commonly occur with downhill skiing, and they less often occur with snowboarding;
however, upper extremity injuries occur more commonly than ACL injuries during
snowboarding.1
Epidemiology
Female athletes have a twofold to eightfold higher risk of ACL injury than male athletes if level
of competition, age, and time exposed are considered.1

Epidemiology
The reason for the higher rate of injuries among females is not clearly understood but is
felt to be because of differences between males and females in neuromuscular firing
patterns in the quadriceps and hamstrings. Potential contributing factors include ACL
size and notch width anatomy, biomechanics, alignment, muscle strength, hormonal
factors, and training.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology

Knowledge of the location of the ACL footprint based on anatomic landmarks is important
(Figure 1).
Figure 1 Photographs show the anatomy of the anterior cruciate ligament. A, With the knee in
extension, the anteromedial (AM) and posterolateral (PL) femoral insertions of the anterior
cruciate ligament are oriented vertically about the posterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle.
B, The AM and PL bundles are parallel to each other, with the PL bundle taut. C, The AM and PL
bundles are named according to their tibial sites of insertion. Note the close approximation to
the anterior and posterior horns of the lateral meniscus. D, With the knee in flexion, the
insertions of the AM and PL bundles are oriented horizontally. E, The bundles cross each other,
with the AM bundle taut. (Reproduced with permission from Honkamp NJ, Shen W, Okeke N,
Ferretti M, Fu FH: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries, in DeLee JC, Drez D Jr, Miller MD, eds:
Orthopaedic Sports Medicine. Philadelphia, PA, WB Saunders, 2010, vol 2, p 1646.)

Osteology
The center of the ACL femoral footprint is 43% of the distance from the proximal-to-
distal articular cartilage margin. The center of the anteromedial bundle is 29.5% of the
proximal-to-distal distance of the lateral femoral intercondylar notch, and the center of

9/3/26, 7:21 AM
AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000539
3/33

the posterolateral bundle is 50% of the same distance. The posterior edge of the ACL is
2.5 mm from the posterior articular cartilage border.2,3 The lateral intercondylar ridge
serves as the anterior border of the footprint. The bifurcate ridge divides the
anteromedial and posterolateral bundles on the femoral side.4 The distance from the
lateral aspect of the articular cartilage of the tibial plateau to the center of the tibial
insertions of the anteromedial and posterolateral bundles is a mean of 44.2% and 52.4%
of the total widest width of the tibial plateau, respectively.5
Vascular Anatomy
The proximal aspect is supplied by the middle genicular artery.
Distally, the ACL is supplied by portions of the medial and lateral inferior genicular artery.

Vascular Anatomy
A synovial plexus with small vessels is parallel to the collagen bundles. Avascularity has
been noted at the insertion sites and areas of the chondrocyte-like cells, lending concern
for potential healing in these regions.6
Neural Anatomy
Few neural receptors are present in the ACL, most of which are Ruffini receptors that function
in stretch and free nerve endings that function as nociceptors.
The remaining mechanoreceptors in the ACL stump have been shown to have a positive
correlation with proprioception.6
Tendons
The ACL consists of type I collagen primarily and type III collagen.
Histologic sections of the portion in direct contact to the intercondylar fossa in full extension
demonstrate tenocytes and chondrocyte-like cells (likely from physiologic impingement).6

Joints and Ligaments
The ACL consists of anteromedial and posterolateral bundles; the former of which is tighter in
knee flexion, and the latter of which is tighter in extension.

Joints and Ligaments
Loading with anterior translation with or without internal rotation places tension on both
bundles. The width ranges from 7 to 12 mm, and the mean length is 32 mm.6
Musculature
Core and hip musculature in addition to quadriceps and hamstrings contribute to stability of
the knee.
The hamstrings serve as a secondary stabilizer to anterior translation of the knee, which is the
reason strengthening may aid in stability and support; this is particularly important in
considering prevention.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most ACL injuries are complete disruptions; however, disruption of a single anatomic bundle
(anteromedial or posterolateral) may occur in 5% to 10% of patients or in as many as 28% of
patients.7,8,9

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
In skeletally mature patients, the femoral insertion or the midsubstance is the most
common site of disruption. In skeletally immature patients, the tibial attachment may be
avulsed with or without a periosteal or osseous fragment.
Risk Factors

5/33

A number of factors may predispose patients to an ACL injury and should be considered in
evaluating for prevention.

Risk Factors
These risk factors include knee valgus moment, smaller notch width index, hormonal
and neuromuscular differences in females versus males, increased tibial slope and
meniscal deficiency. In addition, hyperlaxity/recurvatum, young age, prior ACL rupture,
familial/genetic predisposition, quadriceps dominance, and altered landing mechanics
may be contributing factors.1
Associated Injuries
Surgeons must assess for other ligamentous or meniscal pathology, osteochondral injury, and
subchondral fracture or edema patterns (centrolateral femoral condyle near the sulcus
terminalis and posterolateral tibial plateau).

Associated Injuries
Lateral meniscus tears commonly are associated with acute ACL ruptures, and medial
meniscus tears more often are observed in patients with chronic ACL injuries. Medial
collateral ligament injuries are commonly associated with ACL injuries, and lateral
collateral or posterolateral corner knee injuries must be identified and addressed to
avoid undue stress on the ACL graft.2
Injury Classification
ACL injuries may be classified as occurring from a noncontact or contact mechanism of injury.
Injuries also are graded according to the degree of translation noted on Lachman testing and
pivot-shift testing1 (Table 1).

Mechanics of Fractures
Fractures can occur at the ACL insertion involving the tibial eminence and also may be
observed at the anterolateral tibial plateau (referred to as a Segond fracture). These are
important to recognize because they may alter treatment considerations for certain surgeons.

Mechanics of Fractures
Tibial eminence avulsion fracture fixation versus ACL reconstruction has been shown to
result in lower mean clinical outcome scores compared in patients with an ACL tear at a
minimum follow-up of 2-years. In addition, more postoperative anterior laxity and a
higher rate of postoperative arthrofibrosis have been noted. No difference in
subsequent ACL injury rate has been observed.10
The anterolateral complex (ALC) of the knee provides stability to the lateral knee. The
ALC involves the superficial and deep segments of the iliotibial band, the capsule-
osseous layer (termed by some as the anterolateral ligament [ALL]), and the
anterolateral capsule. The region in which the superficial iliotibial band is linked to the
distal femoral condyle is referred to as Kaplan fibers, which form the proximal aspect of
the ALC.11 Segond fractures, in which an avulsion pattern is observed on the
anterolateral aspect of the tibial plateau with forced internal rotation, can occur.12 Direct
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:21 AM
AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000539
7/33

repair of the Segond fracture while addressing the anterolateral capsule in patients with
an ACL rupture and a high-grade pivot shift results in clinical restoration of rotational
stability. However, the management of Segond fractures is controversial and remains a
subject of debate. Additional research is indicated to determine indications for ALC-
based procedures.12,13
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
An appropriate and detailed patient history may increase suspicion for an ACL injury.

Patient History
A patient who sustains a knee injury during sports activity that is followed by knee
swelling within 1 to 6 hours should be evaluated carefully for a possible ACL injury.
Patients with a chronic ACL injury may report recurrent episodes of knee instability,
mechanical symptoms from a secondary meniscal tear, or pain and swelling. A delay in
diagnosis of 3 to 6 months is associated with a two- to threefold increased risk of
meniscal tear and/or chondral damage because of reliance on secondary stabilizers and
increased shear stress noted. This further emphasizes the importance of the ACL
biomechanically.
Physical Examination
In patients with an acute ACL injury, physical examination may be difficult or limited secondary
to pain.
The best physical examination is performed on the field of competition; after evaluation in the
clinical setting, guarding secondary to increased muscle tone and apprehension may interfere.
An effusion with hemarthrosis secondary to bleeding from the vascular, torn ligament often
occurs.

8/33


Physical Examination
The knee should be palpated carefully, with attention focused on the joint lines and the
origins/insertions of the medial collateral ligament, the posterolateral corner, and the
posterior cruciate ligament (PCL). Patient apprehension on movement of the patella
should be noted because acute patellar dislocations often present with a patient history
that is very similar to that for an ACL injury, and the two injuries may be confused in the
acute setting. The quadriceps and patellar tendons also should be examined in the acute
setting for lack of active knee extension and the presence of a straight leg raise. The
Lachman test is the most useful test for diagnosing ACL injuries in the acute setting. The
knee is flexed to 20° to 30°, and the distal femur is held securely in one hand as the
examiner translates the tibia anteriorly with the other hand. A sense of increased
movement and lack of a solid end point indicate ACL injury. Grades of ACL injury using
the Lachman test are shown in Table 1. The anterior drawer test is performed with the
knee in 90° of flexion. Anterior translation of the tibia is assessed in relation to the distal
femur. The total amount of translation and the quality of the endpoint are assessed in a
manner similar to that for the Lachman test.
The pivot-shift test is pathognomonic for ACL injury. This test is best in the chronic
setting. The pivot-shift test begins with the knee in full extension. The knee is then flexed
as the examiner applies a valgus moment and an axial load. A positive test result occurs
if the anterolateral tibial plateau (which is subluxated anteriorly on the femur) reduces
with a visible shift at the lateral joint line as the iliotibial band passes posterior to the
axis of knee rotation at approximately 15° of knee flexion. Three grades of pivot-shift
injury exist: grade I (pivot glide), grade II (thud-clunk), and grade III (gross). Findings in the
injured knee should always be compared with those on the contralateral side because a
physiologic pivot glide occasionally may be present in individuals with physiologically
laxity.
The medial collateral ligament and the posterolateral ligamentous complex, primarily the
lateral collateral ligament, must be assessed for stability by applying valgus and varus
stress, respectively. The posterolateral ligamentous complex must be examined for
posterolateral rotatory laxity as documented by the dial test, reverse pivot-shift test, and

9/3/26, 7:21 AM
AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000539
9/33

external rotation recurvatum test. The PCL also must be examined. Ideally, this is
performed with the knee in 90° of flexion; however, this maneuver often is difficult in the
acute setting because the patient is in pain.
The patient in whom examination for an acute ACL injury is not clearly positive may have
a partial ACL injury. Physical examination is critical in consideration of partial ACL injuries
because imaging studies may not be definitive.
Partial injuries may not withstand additional trauma, which may contribute to additional
instability. If the examiner suspects a partial injury with plans to proceed surgical
management, diagnostic arthroscopy of the affected knee should be performed before
graft harvest and/or preparation.
Neurovascular Examination
Neurovascular injury must be ruled out by assessing motor and sensory function and pedal
pulses.

Neurovascular Examination
In patients with multiligament injuries from higher-energy trauma, vascular injuries can
occur. Multiligament disruptions (ie, two or more ligaments disrupted) should increase
suspicion for a knee dislocation. With a posterolateral ligamentous complex injury
resulting from varus stress, peroneal nerve injuries also may be detected via loss of
ankle dorsiflexion and eversion and via sensory loss in the first web space and the lateral
aspect of the leg and foot.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs are useful in the acute setting to rule out fracture.

9/3/26, 7:21 AM
AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000539
10/33

In skeletally immature patients, radiographs should be evaluated for open physes, which may
affect surgical treatment options.

Radiography
The most common fracture pattern is a Segond fracture, which is a capsular avulsion off
the lateral tibial plateau that represents an avulsion of the lateral capsule. Tibial
eminence fractures also may be observed on radiographs. In the chronic setting, full-
length plain radiographs may be useful to assess the mechanical axis. Asymmetric genu
varum or genu valgum may reflect medial or lateral compartment degeneration,
respectively, which may result from chronic meniscal and/or articular cartilage damage.
In addition, this may subject ACL injuries to aberrant stresses and, potentially, higher risk
of failure with reconstruction. Sagittal posterior tibial slope also should be assessed
because higher tibial slope has been shown to increase the risk of ACL tear. This is
measured by calculating the angle between the perpendicular axis of the tibial diaphysis
and the line at the superior aspect of the anterior and posterior aspects of the medial
tibial plateau.14
Computed Tomography
CT is more useful in the evaluation of periarticular or avulsion fracture patterns, particularly
tibial eminence fractures.
In general, MRI is more beneficial than CT in the evaluation of associated pathology.
In revision settings, CT will provide insight on the degree of bone loss and tunnel widening and
relative tunnel positioning.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
With a confirmatory examination, MRI is not required for the diagnosis of ACL injury; however,
it is useful in assessing for other ligamentous injury, meniscal pathology, and subchondral
edema or fracture.


Magnetic Resonance Imaging
A characteristic edema pattern observed on MRI, particularly in the acute setting, is
caused by transchondral fractures in the posterolateral tibial plateau and the
anterolateral femoral condyle (near the sulcus terminalis), indicating a rotational event
that likely occurred secondary to an ACL injury (Figure 2). On sagittal and coronal MRIs,
ACL injuries appear as disruptions in the ACL fibers, often with corresponding laxity in
the PCL resting tension. Oblique coronal and sagittal MRIs also can be obtained, which
affords visualization of the longitudinal axis of the ACL. This may improve diagnostic
accuracy of partial and complete ACL ruptures.15

femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau. This type of injury is believed to result from an
anterolateral rotational event of the tibia in reference to the femur secondary to an anterior
cruciate ligament injury. (Reproduced from Hettrich CM, Marx RG, Parker RD, Matava MJ, Sekiya
JK: Ligamentous injuries of the knee, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review,
ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1268-1274.)

Differential Diagnosis
Osteochondral injuries in addition to other ligamentous injuries are critical to identify to
properly manage each injury and achieve the best outcome.

Differential Diagnosis
Acute patellar dislocations, quadriceps or patellar tendon ruptures, or bucket-handle
meniscal tears may share a similar patient history; therefore, a thorough physical
examination is important. PCL injuries may challenge the Lachman examination because
of abnormal posterior tibial station with secondary anterior pseudolaxity.1
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Individualized treatment is appropriate for patients with a partial ACL injury, including those
with a low-energy injury, who may have a good outcome with nonsurgical treatment.
Indications
Nonsurgical management of ACL injuries may be considered in specific subsets of patients if
the risks of surgical management outweigh the advantages. This can be determined from
functional status and activity levels and based on general health and degenerative findings in
the knee.

Indications
Indications include patients participating in low-demand activities, patients who are
older, patients who are sedentary, patients with limited functional instability, patients
with arthritis, patients who participate in straight-line sports activity, and patients who
participate in in activities without frequent cutting/pivoting.1

AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000539
13/33

Contraindications
Contraindications include athletes who participate in sports that involve cutting and pivoting to
avoid instability and secondary meniscal and/or articular cartilage damage.
Techniques/Procedures

Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management involves rehabilitation to strengthen the hamstrings and
quadriceps and proprioceptive training.
Activity modifications, primarily with avoidance of cutting and pivoting activities, also is
an important part of nonsurgical management because patients who avoid these
activities have a lower risk for subsequent knee instability. Functional ACL sports braces
(custom and off-the-shelf) are available; however, they have not been shown to prevent
abnormal anterior tibial translation or decrease the risk of re-injury. These braces and
simple knee sleeves may improve proprioception, which may give patients a sense of
improved knee function and stability.1
Nonsurgical Fracture Fixation
Nondisplaced fractures, particularly in skeletally immature patients, may be amenable to
nonsurgical management; however, close clinical and radiographic follow-up is warranted to
monitor for displacement.
Outcomes
Most patients can function well and perform activities of daily living without instability after a
complete ACL injury.
Some patients have difficulty with simple activities of daily living; because of ACL deficiency–
related instability, these patients may require surgical treatment.
Surgical Management

14/33

Indications
In the acute setting, the decision to reconstruct the ACL generally is related to a patient’s
activity level or anticipated physical demands.

Indications
Patients who are older or less physically active may elect to modify their activities and
proceed with nonsurgical treatment. If nonsurgical treatment fails or knee instability
persists, surgical treatment can be performed. Athletes with an ACL injury who
participate in sports that involve cutting and pivoting, such as basketball, football, and
soccer, usually undergo surgical treatment to avoid instability and secondary meniscal
and/or articular cartilage damage. The decision about whether ACL surgery is needed for
an individual to return to sports activity is not always readily apparent. Many
recreational skiers who do not participate in cutting and pivoting sports can function well
without surgical treatment. Patients with jobs that may involve physical combat (active
military, law enforcement officers), risk (firefighters), or activity on unstable surfaces
(construction workers) may more strongly consider ACL reconstruction before returning
to work.1
Contraindications
Contraindications include lack of quadriceps function, substantial comorbidities, inability to
tolerate the surgical procedure, or unwillingness to complete the rehabilitation program.

Contraindications
After an acute injury, patients should not undergo surgical treatment until the effusion is
controlled and full range of motion (especially extension), good quadriceps function, and
normal gait have been regained. Patients who undergo ACL reconstruction prematurely
may have a higher risk for postoperative arthrofibrosis. Advanced osteoarthritis is a
relative contraindication. Patients with osteoarthritis may have substantial pain, swelling,

9/3/26, 7:21 AM
AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000539
15/33

and limited motion postoperatively despite a stable knee. Therefore, they may not
experience a satisfactory outcome.1
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative imaging studies are helpful if concern exists regarding additional pathology that
needs to be addressed surgically, including meniscal, ligamentous, or osteochondral damage.
Assessment for open physes is crucial to determine the approach for grafts and tunnels.
A preoperative discussion with the patient is important so that graft options and factors that
may affect the condition of the graft may be considered. Surgeons should address risks and
advantages specific to a patient’s level of activity and general health.
Graft choices for ACL reconstruction include autologous options (bone-patellar tendon-bone
[BTB], hamstring tendons, and quadriceps tendon) and allograft tissues (BTB, Achilles tendon,
and tibialis anterior).

Preoperative Planning
In comparing various autograft options, numerous considerations should be discussed
with patients. BTB is associated with less creep and a slightly lower re-rupture rate
compared with hamstring autograft, with no substantial difference in graft survival
compared to quadriceps autograft. Reported complications of BTB include increased
rates of anterior knee pain and slightly higher risk of osteoarthritis. Hamstring autograft
is associated with less donor site morbidity compared and a lower midterm and long-
term incidence of osteoarthritis compared with BTB; however, it is associated with a
longer time to biologic incorporation, weakness with hip extension and terminal knee
flexion, and variable lengths and sizes during harvesting. Lastly, quadriceps autograft
has gained popularity because of its increased relative graft thickness, availability of a
bone block, and higher ultimate load to failure and stiffness compared with BTB. A
potential for anterior knee pain and a risk of knee flexion stiffness and quadriceps
strength deficiency exist16 (Table 2).

Patient Positioning
Perform examination under anesthesia
May apply thigh tourniquet
Position patient supine with a lateral post or an arthroscopic limb holder

Patient Positioning
With the use of a leg post, position the patient closer to the edge of the bed on the side
of the post; move the post to a position that will allow for creation of a valgus stress.
With the use of a leg holder, pad or place nonsurgical leg in a well-leg holder, and lower
the bed so the surgical leg can flex freely to 90°.
Surgical Approaches
Standard diagnostic arthroscopy is initially performed via an anterolateral portal with direct
visualization of the anteromedial portal.
Surgical Procedures
The most important factor is a well-performed, reproducible, and anatomic surgical technique.

Surgical Procedures
Visualization of the femoral and tibial anatomic footprint facilitates appropriate guide
pin placement and tunnel drilling. The ACL originates at the posterior aspect of the
medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle and travels obliquely distal-anterior-medial
to the space between the medial and lateral tibial spines. The anterior edge of the PCL
and the posterior aspect of the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus also have been
used as landmarks, keeping in mind variants of normal anatomy.6 Virtually all ACL
reconstruction procedures are performed as an outpatient arthroscopic procedure.
Most procedures are performed via an arthroscopic technique in which the femoral
tunnel is drilled from inside the joint. Some surgeons prefer to drill the femoral tunnel
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:21 AM
AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000539
18/33

from outside-in, which necessitates a second incision. No clinical difference exists
between the two techniques. Other techniques involve an anteromedial
portal/transportal technique, transtibial technique, and two-incision technique/outside-
in. An additional technique described involves avoidance of drilling a femoral tunnel and
performing an over-the-top femoral approach, in which the graft is passed over the
lateral femoral condyle and fixed to the lateral femoral cortex.20
Increased conversion to drilling the femoral tunnel via a tibial tunnel–independent
technique, most notably via the anteromedial portal or the outside-in technique, has
occurred. The transtibial method may more frequently result in a femoral tunnel that is
too vertical, re-creating a nonanatomic or high anteromedial tunnel with inadequate
graft obliquity and stability with rotational movement. Conversely, the anteromedial
portal, via retrograde/outside-in drilling methods, allows for more reliable placement of
the femoral tunnel at the native ACL footprint (more obliquely down the intercondylar
wall) than that reliably achieved via transtibial drilling. This potentially results in
improved rotational stability. Drilling through an anteromedial portal requires knee
hyperflexion (>110°) to avoid posterior femoral wall blow-out. Anteromedial portal

femoral tunnel than that achieved via transtibial or outside-in reaming (Video 1).

A renewed interest exists in ACL repair in select patients based on limited short-term

in younger patients with an acute femoral-sided injury or periosteal and osseous

and biomechanical strength; however, its presence may lead to stress shielding on the
biologic graft. The repaired ACL remains weaker than the native ACL. Although current
evidence suggests that primary ACL repair can achieve some favorable initial, short-term
results, outcomes have deteriorated, with comparatively higher failure rates and
persistent instability noted at midterm to long-term follow-up. Therefore, consideration
of primary repair is reserved for a narrowly selected subset of patients, whereas ACL
reconstruction remains the preferred treatment option for more consistent surgical
outcomes.21,22

advocated in an attempt to confer increased rotational stability to the knee and a higher
rate of return to sports activity above that offered by ACL reconstruction alone.
Suggested indications (level V) for a combined ALL and ACL reconstruction include the
following:
Revision ACL reconstruction
Grade III pivot shift
Genu recurvatum (>10° of hyperextension) or generalized ligamentous laxity

Postoperatively, patients are allowed to bear weight as tolerated with the use of crutches until

Concurrent meniscal or articular cartilage procedures may affect weight-bearing status.

Avoiding common errors to ensure an anatomic technique in addition to addressing all

Careful evaluation of tunnel positioning is critical to avoid error. Perform a thorough
assessment for additional pathology because lack of recognition to concomitantly
address additional pathology may lead to failed reconstruction. Preoperative
optimization is key, from range of motion goals to modifiable risk factors; tobacco use,
infection, and wound complications have been shown to increase postoperative anterior
translation and knee instability after ACL reconstruction with BTB autograft.2
Complications
DVT/Venous Thromboembolism
DVT is not uncommon after ACL reconstruction, with reported rates as high as 9% and varying
degrees of symptomatic involvement. Conversely, thromboembolic disease occurs less
frequently (0.1% to 0.2%). Anticoagulation may be considered in patients with a history of DVT,
females who use oral contraceptives, and patients with a family history of
hypercoagulability.31,32
Arthrofibrosis
Knee stiffness generally is uncommon and usually resolves via physical therapy. Stiffness is
more common after multiligament reconstruction; in some patients, manipulation under
anesthesia may be necessary. Retropatellar fat pad fibrosis may require repeat arthroscopy
with lysis of adhesions, careful scrutiny to address any cyclops lesions, and anterior interval
release.
Pain
Postoperative pain is expected and may be better managed via regional blocks and/or a
multimodal pain management approach.
Incorporation of modalities, including NSAIDs and cryotherapy, are beneficial in recovery.
Re-tear
A level I study reported a failure rate of 20% in 18-year-old patients who were treated via an
allograft versus 6% in patients who were treated via an autograft.1 In 40-year-old patients, a

Graft-screw divergence greater than 15° to 30° may lead to failure.33
Hardware Malpositioning
Painful hardware at the proximal tibia near the tibial tunnel (particularly cortical screw or
staple fixation), if sufficiently disabling, may result in secondary surgery for hardware removal.
Fracture
Lateral cortex or posterior (proximal) wall blowout may occur if drilling; visualization is
important. In these patients, an extended button or aperture fixation may be considered.
Instability
Instability may be related to graft malpositioning or additional ligamentous injury that was not
recognized and addressed.

Deep infection after ACL reconstruction is uncommon (0.8%).

If deep infection occurs, repeat arthroscopy may be required for irrigation and
débridement and possible hardware removal and graft removal to eradicate the
infection. Deep infections involving the knee are also managed via 6 weeks of
intravenous antibiotic therapy. Hamstring autograft is associated with a higher rate of
infection.16

Uncommonly, an aseptic soft-tissue reaction may be observed in patients after allograft

This may be considered in patients with recurrent effusions in whom infection and other
potential causes have been ruled out.
Effusion
A postoperative effusion is expected to resorb with time; however, persistent effusion may
indicate potential problems, such as infection, arthrofibrosis, or reinjury.
Hematoma
Hematoma may occur postoperatively and should be monitored more closely if not resolving,
particularly in patients being treated with the use of stronger/long-term anticoagulants.
If painful and/or obstructing range of motion, consider early aspiration.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Saphenous neuritis, in addition to damage to the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve,
may occur with hamstring harvest.
Other Complications
Anesthesia-related complications (eg, pain related to a spinal or epidural block, spinal
headache, femoral nerve palsy after regional block, or major respiratory or allergic problems
secondary to general anesthesia) may occur.
Lack of full extension occurs in approximately 4% of patients.
Revision surgery
In evaluating failed ACL reconstruction, the surgeon must attempt to determine the etiology
of failure.
Revision surgery is more technically demanding because of prior tunnels and hardware.

Lack of extension is more common after multiligament reconstruction. In some patients,
manipulation under anesthesia or revision surgery may be required for persistent
arthrofibrosis. Loss of full extension may occur secondary to scarring from the graft or if
remaining ACL tissue scars and forms a cyclops lesion (nodular scar tissue formed
anterior to the ACL graft, blocking extension). This may require secondary surgery to
remove the tissue that blocks full extension.
Graft failure is classified as biologic, traumatic, or related to technical failure. Based on
the Multicenter ACL Revision Study database, outcomes after ACL revision surgery
appear to be inferior to those after primary ACL reconstruction.1 Combination failure
from more than one cause was most commonly noted. Femoral tunnel malpositioning
from technical error was documented in 80% of patients. Intra-articular pathology in the
form of articular cartilage damage of all cartilage surfaces is higher in patients who
undergo ACL revision surgery than in patients who undergo primary ACL reconstruction.
Prior partial meniscectomy portends a poor prognosis with regard to articular cartilage
damage in revision procedures. Higher rates of primary graft failure have been observed
in patients with hyperlaxity who undergo allograft reconstruction. The surgeon is the
most important factor influencing graft selection for ACL revision surgery.1
Rehabilitation
Studies have shown that a knee immobilizer or continuous passive motion machine is not
required postoperatively.1,35
Patients are encouraged to emphasize closed chain strengthening. They are permitted to
begin light running between 3 and 4 months postoperatively if strengthening has progressed
sufficiently.


Outcomes
Reconstruction of the ACL generally results in excellent outcomes; however, many patients
have slightly decreased levels of activity.
The use of the one-incision technique versus the two-incision technique does not appear to
affect outcomes.
Re-rupture rates range from 1% to 20% in the literature.1

Outcomes
KT-1000 arthrometer testing shows a 1- to 2-mm difference in side-to-side laxity, which is
not clinically important. The risk of future radiographic osteoarthritis after ACL
reconstruction ranges from zero to 13% in patients with an isolated ACL tear and 21% to
48% in patients with an ACL tear and a meniscal tear. ROM will return to normal.
Isokinetic strength will be greater than 90% of normal. A contralateral ACL tear will occur
in 3% to 6% of patients. No clinically or substantially relevant differences exist in
instrumented laxity, patient-reported outcomes, or quadriceps or hamstring strength
between BTB autograft and hamstring tendon autograft. Kneeling pain is more common
with BTB autograft; however, return to elite-level sports activity also is somewhat higher
with BTB autograft. In the past few years, the use of allograft has increased in the United
States. A meta-analysis showed that older patients who underwent ACL reconstruction
with the use of an allograft were more likely to experience graft re-rupture and have
greater asymmetry in their hop test (>10% side-to-side difference) than patients who
underwent autograft reconstruction.1,36 Excluding irradiated and chemically processed
grafts from the analysis, no substantial differences were found in graft rupture; revision
surgery; International Knee Documentation Committee scores, Lachman, pivot-shift, or
hop test results; patellar crepitus; or return to sports activity. Based on the growing body

indications for ALL reconstruction continued to be defined. 1
Pearls and Pitfalls
Tunnel placement is the most critical aspect of ACL reconstruction.
The most common error in ACL reconstruction is placing the femoral tunnel too anteriorly,
resulting in decreased range of motion, altered kinematics, and ultimately graft failure.

Pearls and Pitfalls
With a single-incision transtibial technique, the tibial tunnel should begin at the anterior
aspect of the tibial insertion of the medial collateral ligament to allow the graft to be
placed obliquely and arrive at the 10:30-o’clock or 1:30-o’clock position on the
intercondylar notch of the femur. If the tibial tunnel is drilled too anteriorly on the tibia,
the graft will be vertically placed, which is not desirable (although this is less common).
Surgeons must understand that the direction of the tibial tunnel influences femoral
tunnel placement if using a single-incision technique (if the femoral tunnel is drilled
through the tibial tunnel). This problem can be avoided by drilling the femoral tunnel
through a medial portal or by using a two-incision technique.1
